title: What is known about 1RB0RE_1LC0RA_0LD1LB_1LA1LE_0LB0LF_1LD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RE_1LC0RA_0LD1LB_1LA1LE_0LB0LF_1LD---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open; the phase map is now proved far beyond the first m ≡ 2 case. The tape at a phase start is A> 1110 10 1m followed by a list of remnants 0 (10)k 1c. Lean proves a phase map on (m, remnant list) with exact step counts that covers every case except m ≡ 2 (mod 3) in front of a remnant with c = 2 (or in front of a non-final remnant with c ≤ 1). In particular the m ≡ 2 case of a clean phase is S(3j+2) → S(10j−2) followed by the remnant 0 (10)6 1111 (j ≥ 2). From blank tape the proved map carries the run through 61,963 phases (m of 107,632 bits), so if the machine halts it does so after more than 26953 steps (kernel) / 2215260 steps (compiled evaluation). Phase 61,964 is the first uncovered case: m ≡ 2 in front of the remnant 0 (10)75 11.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The round, and the end of a phase
claims.text: Write T(x, m, R) for the tape 1 1 1 0 (10)x 1m R with the head in A at its left end. One round: T(x, m+3, R) → T(x+5, m, R) in 6x + 51 steps. With no 1s left, (10)x becomes C> (11)x+6 (4x + 37 steps); with one 1 left, C> (11)x+7 (4x + 41 steps); and C> 1 1 at the left end restarts with x = 1 (16 steps).

claims.title: The phase map
claims.text: With S(m) = 0∞ A> 1 1 1 0 1 0 1m 0∞: S(3j) reaches S(10j + 12) and S(3j + 1) reaches S(10j + 14).

claims.title: No halt before S(31,957,652)
claims.text: The machine reaches S(12) in 75 steps and then, by the map, S(52), S(184), S(624), S(2,092), S(6,984), S(23,292), S(77,652), S(258,852), S(862,852), S(2,876,184), S(9,587,292), S(31,957,652). Adding the proved step counts gives step 168,344,857,095,747 for the last one (the Lean theorem states that it is reached; the count is from py/orbit.py, and the first four agree with a direct run: 620, 6,070, 65,728).

claims.title: Where it can halt
claims.text: Only F reading 1 halts; F is entered only from E reading 1 (0LF), so the machine halts exactly on 1 E> 1. Read off the table.

claims.title: The case m ≡ 2 (mod 3), and phases in front of remnants
claims.text: With the remnant G(k, c) = 0 (10)k 1c and P(m, W) = A> 1110 10 1m followed by the remnants W: after the rounds (x' = x + 5⌊m/3⌋), m ≡ 0 sends G(k+1, c) to P(2x'+11, G(k, c)…) and G(0, c) to P(2x'+10+c, …); m ≡ 1 joins the first remnant to the phase (the tape is T(x'+k+1, c)); m ≡ 2 with x' ≥ 8 gives P(2x'−4, [G(6, 4)]) on blank tape, P(2x', G(k+7, c)…) before G(k, c+3), and P(2x'−4, [G(6, 2k+4)]) / P(2x'−4, [G(6, 2k+6)]) before a last G(k, 0) / G(k, 1). Each case is a run of the machine with its exact step count. For a clean phase: S(3j+2) → P(10j−2, [G(6, 4)]) for j ≥ 2.

claims.title: If it halts, it takes more than 2<sup>6953</sup> steps
claims.text: Iterating the proved map from S(12) (step 75), every phase start it reaches is a configuration of the run at the computed step (orbit_reaches), and a halt comes after all of them (lt_of_halts). The kernel evaluates 2,000 phases: step > 26953.

claims.title: 61,963 phases: a halt takes more than 2<sup>215260</sup> steps
claims.text: The same, evaluated by compiled code through 61,963 phases (m then has 107,632 bits). The next phase is the first case the map does not cover: m ≡ 2 (mod 3) in front of the remnant 0 (10)75 11.

claims.title: The uncovered case: m ≡ 2 before a remnant with c = 2
claims.text: There the leftover pair of 1s meets the remnant's pair, and small runs show a nested process whose outcome depends on k (from T(10, 2) before G(k, 2): k = 0 → P(26, [G(1, 7)]), k = 1 → P(18, [G(9, 1)]), k = 2 → a phase T(17, 4) with no remnant, k = 3 → P(26, [G(0, 2), G(4, 4)]), k = 4 → P(16, [G(13, 1)])). Its rule was not worked out. Before the remnant rules: direct runs S(2) → S(28), S(5) → S(112), S(8) → S(276), S(11) → S(128), S(20) → S(228), S(29) → S(328).

claims.title: No closed tape language with small windows
claims.text: bbtools.ctl K = 3..6 leaves halting configurations; n-gram CPS widths 3 to 7 fails; no invariant a·ones + b·pos + W mod 2..12.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 82,012 cells have been visited and 78,899 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.487). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.032).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The proved map covers the run through 61,963 phases; whether the machine halts depends on the nested case (m ≡ 2 before a remnant with c = 2) and on the cases after it. The machine can stop only on 1 E> 1, which none of the proved cases produce.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The machine runs a Collatz-like map on the number of 1s (about ×10/3 per phase), and when the count is 2 mod 3 it leaves a small remnant on the tape that later phases absorb. Lean proves the map, remnants included, through 61,963 phases from blank tape: if it ever halts, it takes more than 2^6953 steps.

facts.text: A halt, if any, comes later (2,000 proved phases).
Covered by the proved map; a halt would take over 2<sup>215260</sup> steps.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A stack of 10s and a run of 1s
html:
At the start of every phase the whole tape is

A> 1 1 1 0 1 0 1^m

with the head in state A at the left end; call it S(m). From blank tape the machine reaches S(12) after 75 steps, S(52) after 620, S(184) after 6,070, S(624) after 65,728. Within a phase the tape is 1 1 1 0 (10)x 1m: a growing stack of 10s on the left eating a run of 1s on the right.

sections.heading: Three 1s buy five 10s
html:
Each round the head runs from the left end to the first 1s and back: three 1s disappear and five copies of 10 appear, so the tape grows by 7 cells (proved: T(x, m+3) → T(x+5, m) in 6x + 51 steps). When fewer than three 1s are left the phase ends. With none or one left, every 10 turns into 11 and a new phase starts with x = 1:

  • S(3j) → S(10j + 12)
  • S(3j + 1) → S(10j + 14)

Example: S(52), 52 = 3·17 + 1. After 17 rounds the stack is (10)86 with one 1 left; the tape becomes (11)93, and the restart gives S(184) = S(10·17 + 14).
So the count of 1s grows by a factor about 10/3 per phase, and the phase takes about 15j2 steps; that is why the tape grows like the square root of time.

sections.heading: The orbit, and the remnants
html: From 12 the map gives 52, 184, 624, 2,092, 6,984, 23,292, 77,652, 258,852, 862,852, 2,876,184, 9,587,292, 31,957,652. The last is the first ≡ 2 (mod 3): then two 1s are left over after the rounds. Lean proves what happens (phase2_clean): S(3j+2) becomes S(10j−2) followed by a remnant 0 (10)6 1111, so phase 13 is A> 1110 10 1106525498 0 (10)6 1111.

A remnant 0 (10)k 1c looks like a frozen piece of a phase, and the next phases treat it that way. With m ≡ 0 the last 10s of the stack absorb one 10 of the remnant (k goes down by one). With m ≡ 1 the remnant simply joins the phase: … (10)x 1 0 (10)k 1c is the same tape as a phase with x + k + 1 tens and c ones. With m ≡ 2 a new remnant is made, or the old one grows (k + 7, c − 3).

All these cases are proved in Lean with exact step counts (lean/Remnant.lean). Iterating them from blank tape covers 61,963 phases, until the count of 1s has 107,632 bits; the proof of the halting-time bound evaluates 2,000 of them in Lean's kernel (26953 steps) and all of them by compiled code (2215260).

Phase 61,964 is the first case not covered: two leftover 1s in front of a remnant that also ends in two 1s, 0 (10)75 11. Small runs of this case show remnants nesting inside each other; its rule is the next thing to work out. The machine can only stop on 1 E> 1, which none of the proved cases produce.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.487). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.032).
After 109 steps the tape spans 82,012 cells (61,506 left of the start, 11 right), with a density of 1s of 0.962.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A Collatz-like map on the number of 1s with remnants left on the tape: S(3j) → S(10j+12), S(3j+1) → S(10j+14), S(3j+2) → S(10j−2) plus a remnant 0(10)^6 1111; the map on (m, remnants) is proved in Lean through 61,963 phases from blank tape (a halt would take over 2^6953 steps), then hits an unproved nested-remnant case.
